title: Fix zero deletion cost in Python Levenshtein distance
body:
The Python Levenshtein implementation raises `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero` when the deletion cost is zero. Initialize the distance row by multiplication so zero-cost deletion works as it does in the native implementation.

Adds direct Python and public-dispatch regressions for scores, cutoffs and process APIs. The full test suite passed against a native build of this branch, along with the focused Python tests, Black and Ruff.

title: docs: recover matching substrings from extracted choices
body:
Show how to recover matching substrings from `process.extract` results using `fuzz.partial_ratio_alignment` on the selected choices (#394). The example keeps the native implementation, uses the same partial-ratio scorer in both steps, and preserves mapping keys.

Explain which ranges belong to the query and choice, why this does not describe arbitrary scorers such as WRatio, and why offsets from processed strings cannot generally slice the originals. This is a recipe using existing APIs; it does not change the result tuple or avoid the second alignment calculation.

Validation on Python 3.12/Linux arm64: built native extensions from this checkout, all 421 tests pass, exact doctests pass in native and Python modes, additional checks cover mapping/list inputs, Unicode, empty/no-match inputs, long/short queries, and normalization offsets. Sphinx builds with warnings as errors; all applicable changed-file pre-commit checks pass.

AI-assisted contribution, investigated and validated with Codex.

title: Feature Request: Integration of the new almost-linear edit distance approximation scheme
body:
Hi maintainers,

First of all, thank you for maintaining `rapidfuzz` and `python-Levenshtein`. It is the gold standard for string matching in the Python ecosystem, and I rely on it heavily.

I am writing to bring a recent theoretical breakthrough to your attention and to ask if you would consider evaluating it for potential integration into the library.

### The Context
On September 24, 2026, a manuscript titled **"An Almost-Linear Approximation Scheme for Edit Distance"** was published (attributed to OpenAI / Result 121 in the recent mathematics manuscript collection). 

You can read the full paper here:  https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/An-Almost-Linear-Approximation-Scheme-for-Edit-Distance-September-24-2026/paper.pdf

### The Breakthrough
Historically, computing the exact edit distance requires $O(N^2)$ time (Wagner-Fischer), or $O(N \cdot k)$ for bounded distance (Ukkonen/Myers). Previous approximation algorithms either had polynomial factors depending on $\varepsilon$ (like $N^{1+\xi}$) or were limited to specific regimes.

This new paper presents a **uniform randomized algorithm** that, for any fixed rational $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$, estimates the unit-cost edit distance within a factor of $(1+\varepsilon)$ with probability at least $2/3$, in worst-case expected time **$N^{1+o(1)}$**.

Key technical aspects from the paper:
*   It uses a hierarchical interval decomposition (shift tree) adapted from Andoni-Krauthgamer-Onak.
*   It introduces "cost-weighted curvature" predictions to restrict alignment paths to narrow bands.
*   It uses entropy-regularized online learning (Frank-Wolfe) to select actions within these bands.
*   It relies on lazy evaluation to keep the expected work bound near-linear.

### Why this matters for `rapidfuzz`
Currently, for very long strings (e.g., genomic sequences or large documents) where an exact score isn't strictly necessary but a close approximation is, users are stuck with either:
1.  Exact algorithms that are too slow ($O(N^2)$ or high $O(N \cdot k)$.
2.  Heuristics that lack formal accuracy guarantees.

This algorithm provides a **formal $(1+\varepsilon)$ guarantee** in almost-linear time. Even with the $N^{1+o(1)}$ overhead and constants, for sufficiently large $N$, this would be asymptotically faster than any exact method available today.

### Proposal
I understand that `rapidfuzz` prioritizes extreme performance on small-to-medium strings and deterministic behavior. This algorithm is randomized and likely has high constant factors due to its complexity. 

However, would you be open to:
1.  Reviewing the paper to assess its practical implementability in C++?
2.  Considering it as an optional backend (e.g., `ratio(..., approximate=True, epsilon=0.1)`) specifically targeted at very long inputs where $O(N^2)$ is prohibitive?
3.  Or perhaps pointing to a reference implementation if one becomes available?

I believe this represents the most significant advancement in edit distance algorithms in decades, and having it in `rapidfuzz` would be a huge win for the Python data science and bioinformatics communities.

Thank you for your time and for your incredible work on this library!
